subsections.subsection_title: 1. Medical and Surgical Causes of Pleural Effusion (By System)

items.text: Complications of central venous catheter insertion.
Postoperative anastomotic leak or oesophageal perforation.
Heart failure (can be unilateral, often right-sided).
Nephrotic syndrome or renal failure (occasionally unilateral).
Chylothorax from thoracic duct injury or obstruction.
Complication of central venous catheter insertion.
Complication of thoracentesis or lung biopsy.
Unilateral absent or markedly reduced breath sounds.
Distended neck veins (may be absent in hypovolaemia).
Tracheal deviation away from affected side (late and unreliable sign).
Immediate decompression when clinically suspected; do not wait for X-ray.
Needle decompression using an appropriate large-bore cannula at the locally recommended site, or finger/open thoracostomy by trained personnel.
Support circulation and treat associated injuries.
Reassess immediately for clinical improvement and drain function.
Mediastinal shift away from a massive effusion
Reduced visibility of underlying lung markings
Diffuse haziness of the affected hemithorax
Increased density without a clear meniscus
Lateral displacement of the diaphragmatic dome
Increased distance between the apparent diaphragm and gastric air bubble on the left
Reduced chest expansion on affected side.
Tracheal deviation away from affected side (massive effusion).
Bronchial breathing/egophony just above the effusion.
Homogeneous opacity at the lung base.
Mediastinal shift away from the affected side if massive.
Subpulmonic effusion: apparent elevation of the hemidiaphragm.
Supine film: diffuse hazy opacity without a clear meniscus.
Small, asymptomatic effusion: observation and treatment of cause.
Parapneumonic effusion/empyema: antibiotics ± chest tube drainage.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion: chest tube ± intrapleural tPA/DNase.
Recurrent malignant effusion: indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis.
Heart failure-related effusion: diuretics and heart failure treatment.
Tuberculous effusion: anti-tuberculosis therapy according to guidelines.
Massive effusion: controlled drainage with monitoring for re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Chronic kidney disease with fluid overload.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Causes of Air Bronchogram on CT

items.text: Severe pneumonia with low oxygen saturation
Major trauma or resuscitation when clinically indicated
Pulmonary oxygen toxicity with prolonged high concentrations
Dryness and irritation of nasal mucosa
Retinopathy of prematurity in susceptible neonates
Delayed recognition of deterioration if oxygen masks hypoventilation
Oxygen-induced worsening of hypercapnia in susceptible COPD patients
Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure: usually 88–92% pending blood gas assessment and individualised targets11. Causes of Apnoea
Gastrointestinal reflux-associated events in selected cases
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return with obstruction
Cardiac tamponade in severe circulatory compromise
Central cyanosis: tongue and mucous membranes involved
Peripheral cyanosis: extremities, often with cold skin; tongue usually remains pink

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Unilateral wheeze suggests foreign body aspiration or focal airway obstruction. A silent chest in severe asthma is a life-threatening sign.

items.text: Inspiratory stridor: usually extrathoracic upper airway obstruction
Expiratory stridor: usually intrathoracic airway obstruction
Biphasic stridor: fixed obstruction at the glottis or subglottis
